content: Newborn infants are more susceptible to seizures compared to older children and adults. Seizures in neonates can lead to significant neuronal injury, often resulting in long-term neurodevelopmental impairments. While there are several anti-seizure medications (ASMs) available for neonates, the optimal choice for first-line, second-line, and third-line treatment remains uncertain. Additionally, other aspects of seizure management, such as whether ASMs should be initiated for electrographic-only seizures and the appropriate duration of ASM therapy after achieving seizure control, are not well-defined. The primary objective of this review was to determine whether any specific ASM is more or less effective than another when used as first-line, second-line, or third-line treatment in controlling seizures and improving neurodevelopmental outcomes in neonates. The analysis separately evaluated seizures confirmed by electroencephalography (EEG) and those diagnosed clinically. The second objective was to assess the impact of maintenance therapy with ASMs compared to no maintenance therapy after achieving seizure control. The third objective was to evaluate the treatment of both clinical and electrographic seizures versus the treatment of clinical seizures alone. A comprehensive search of databases, including MEDLINE, Embase, CENTRAL, and others, was conducted in May 2022 and June 2023. Only randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving neonates with EEG-confirmed or clinically diagnosed seizures were included. The trials compared (1) one ASM versus another, (2) maintenance therapy with ASM versus no maintenance therapy, and (3) treatment of both clinical and electrographic seizures versus treatment of clinical seizures alone. Two independent reviewers assessed trial eligibility, risk of bias, and extracted data. Treatment effects were analyzed using risk ratios (RR) for dichotomous outcomes and mean differences (MD) for continuous outcomes, with 95% confidence intervals (CI). The certainty of evidence was evaluated using the GRADE approach. Eighteen trials involving 1,342 neonates were included in the review. Key findings are as follows: 1. Phenobarbital versus Levetiracetam as First-Line ASM in EEG-Confirmed Neonatal Seizures Phenobarbital is likely more effective than levetiracetam in achieving seizure control after the first loading dose (RR 2.32, 95% CI 1.63 to 3.30; moderate-certainty evidence) and after the maximal loading dose (RR 2.83, 95% CI 1.78 to 4.50; moderate-certainty evidence). However, the effect of phenobarbital compared to levetiracetam on mortality before discharge (RR 0.30, 95% CI 0.04 to 2.52), the need for mechanical ventilation (RR 1.21, 95% CI 0.76 to 1.91), sedation or drowsiness (RR 1.74, 95% CI 0.68 to 4.44), and post-discharge epilepsy (RR 0.92, 95% CI 0.48 to 1.76) is uncertain due to very low-certainty evidence. The trial did not report on mortality or neurodevelopmental disability at 18 to 24 months. 2. Phenobarbital versus Phenytoin as First-Line ASM in EEG-Confirmed Neonatal Seizures The effect of phenobarbital compared to phenytoin on achieving seizure control after the maximal loading dose is uncertain (RR 0.97, 95% CI 0.54 to 1.72; very low-certainty evidence). The trial did not report on mortality or neurodevelopmental disability at 18 to 24 months. 3. Maintenance Therapy with ASM versus No Maintenance Therapy in Clinically Diagnosed Neonatal Seizures The effect of short-term maintenance therapy with ASM (discontinued before discharge) compared to no maintenance therapy on the risk of repeat seizures before hospital discharge is uncertain (RR 0.76, 95% CI 0.56 to 1.01; very low-certainty evidence). Maintenance therapy may have little or no effect on mortality before discharge (RR 0.69, 95% CI 0.39 to 1.22; low-certainty evidence), mortality at 18 to 24 months (RR 0.94, 95% CI 0.34 to 2.61; low-certainty evidence), neurodevelopmental disability at 18 to 24 months (RR 0.89, 95% CI 0.13 to 6.12; low-certainty evidence), and post-discharge epilepsy (RR 3.18, 95% CI 0.69 to 14.72; low-certainty evidence). 4. Treatment of Both Clinical and Electrographic Seizures versus Treatment of Clinical Seizures Alone in Neonates Treating both clinical and electrographic seizures compared to treating clinical seizures alone may have little or no effect on seizure burden during hospitalization (MD -1871.16, 95% CI -4525.05 to 782.73; low-certainty evidence), mortality before discharge (RR 0.59, 95% CI 0.28 to 1.27; low-certainty evidence), and post-discharge epilepsy (RR 0.75, 95% CI 0.12 to 4.73; low-certainty evidence). The trials did not report on mortality or neurodevelopmental disability at 18 to 24 months. In conclusion, phenobarbital appears to be more effective than levetiracetam in achieving seizure control as a first-line ASM in neonates with EEG-confirmed seizures. However, there is limited and very low-certainty evidence regarding the effects of different ASMs on other shortand long-term outcomes. Maintenance therapy with ASM after achieving seizure control may have little or no effect on mortality, neurodevelopmental disability, or post-discharge epilepsy. Treating both clinical and electrographic seizures compared to clinical seizures alone may also have little or no effect on key outcomes. These findings are applicable only to term and late preterm neonates. Further well-designed RCTs are needed to address these questions, particularly in preterm infants, and should focus on long-term neurodevelopmental outcomes using EEG-confirmed diagnoses.
